CHAPTER 20 - WAVE PHENOMENA AND LIGHT (WAVE OPTICS)

Introduction

In earlier chapters light was treated as rays that travel in straight lines, obeying the laws of reflection and refraction. Ray (geometrical) optics explains mirrors, lenses and image formation, but it cannot explain what happens when light meets obstacles or apertures comparable in size to its wavelength. Phenomena such as interference, diffraction and polarization show that light is a WAVE. This chapter develops the wave theory of light, starting from Huygens' principle, and uses it to explain reflection, refraction, interference (Young's double-slit experiment), diffraction at a single slit, and polarization (Malus's law, Brewster's law).

20.1 WAVE NATURE OF LIGHT

Newton pictured light as a stream of tiny particles (corpuscles). In 1678 Christiaan Huygens proposed instead that light is a wave. The particle model could not explain interference and diffraction, whereas the wave model could. In the 19th century Thomas Young (interference) and Augustin Fresnel (diffraction) gave decisive experimental support for the wave theory, and Maxwell later showed light is an ELECTROMAGNETIC wave. Light in vacuum travels at c = 3 x 10^8 m/s. Visible light has wavelength lambda roughly 400 nm (violet) to 700 nm (red). Because these wavelengths are so small, wave effects are seen only with small apertures or fine structures.

20.2 WAVEFRONTS

A WAVEFRONT is a surface on which all points vibrate in the same phase. It is the locus of points that the disturbance has reached at the same instant, all oscillating together. The direction of propagation of the wave is always PERPENDICULAR (normal) to the wavefront; such a normal line is called a RAY.
 - A point source in a uniform medium sends out SPHERICAL wavefronts (concentric spheres).
 - A line source produces CYLINDRICAL wavefronts.
 - Far from a small source (or from a source at infinity), a small portion of a spherical wavefront is almost flat - a PLANE wavefront. Parallel rays correspond to plane wavefronts.

20.3 HUYGENS' PRINCIPLE

Huygens' principle is a geometrical construction that tells us how a wavefront advances:
 (1) Every point on a given wavefront acts as a source of secondary wavelets (secondary disturbances) that spread out in the forward direction with the speed of the wave in that medium.
 (2) After a time t, the new wavefront is the surface that touches (is tangent to) all these secondary wavelets - the forward common tangent, called the envelope.
To construct the next wavefront: from each point of the old wavefront draw a small sphere (in 2-D, a circle) of radius v*t (v = wave speed, t = time). The envelope of all these spheres in the forward direction is the new wavefront. The backward envelope is ignored (no back-travelling wave is observed).

20.4 REFLECTION BY HUYGENS' PRINCIPLE

Consider a plane wavefront AB striking a plane reflecting surface. Different parts of the wavefront reach the surface at different times and each point sends out secondary wavelets into the SAME medium (so they travel with the same speed v). By the time the edge B reaches the surface at B', the wavelet from A has expanded to radius equal to BB'. Drawing the common tangent gives the reflected wavefront. Geometry of the two congruent right triangles shows that the angle of incidence i equals the angle of reflection r, and that the incident ray, the reflected ray and the normal lie in one plane. Thus the wave theory reproduces the LAWS OF REFLECTION.

20.5 REFRACTION BY HUYGENS' PRINCIPLE (SNELL'S LAW)

Now let a plane wavefront pass from medium 1 (speed v1) into a denser medium 2 (speed v2 < v1). While the wavelet from one edge travels a distance v1*t in medium 1, the wavelet from the other edge, having already entered medium 2, travels only v2*t. Constructing the new wavefront and using the geometry gives
   sin i / sin r = v1 / v2 = n2 / n1 = constant,
which is SNELL'S LAW. Here n = c/v is the refractive index. Because v2 < v1 in a denser medium, the ray bends TOWARD the normal. Important consequences: when light goes into a denser medium its SPEED and WAVELENGTH decrease (lambda_medium = lambda_vacuum / n) but its FREQUENCY stays the same (frequency is fixed by the source). The wave theory thus correctly predicts that light slows down in a denser medium - the opposite of Newton's corpuscular prediction.

20.6 COHERENT SOURCES AND INTERFERENCE

INTERFERENCE is the modification of intensity produced when two (or more) waves of the same frequency overlap. By the superposition principle the resultant displacement is the sum of the individual displacements. Where crests meet crests the waves reinforce (CONSTRUCTIVE interference, bright); where a crest meets a trough they cancel (DESTRUCTIVE interference, dark).
For a steady (sustained) interference pattern the two sources must be COHERENT: they must have
 - the SAME frequency (and wavelength), and
 - a CONSTANT phase difference that does not change with time.
Two independent lamps are NOT coherent (their phases fluctuate randomly in about 10^-8 s), so they give no steady pattern. Coherent sources are obtained by DERIVING two sources from a single source - e.g. the two slits in Young's experiment, illuminated by the same wavefront. For good contrast the two beams should also have nearly equal amplitude and (for unpolarized light) the same polarization.
Path difference and phase difference are linked by:  phase difference = (2*pi / lambda) x path difference.
 - Constructive (bright): path difference = n*lambda   (n = 0, 1, 2, ...).
 - Destructive (dark):   path difference = (n + 1/2)*lambda = (2n - 1)*lambda/2.
Interference redistributes energy - it is neither created nor destroyed; the energy missing from the dark fringes appears in the bright fringes, so energy is conserved.

20.7 YOUNG'S DOUBLE-SLIT EXPERIMENT (YDSE)

Thomas Young (1801) let light from a single narrow slit fall on two close, parallel slits S1 and S2 (separation d). The two slits act as coherent sources and their overlapping waves fall on a screen at distance D. Alternate bright and dark bands - FRINGES - appear.
Take a point P on the screen at distance x from the centre O (the point equidistant from the slits). The path difference is
   S2P - S1P = d sin theta  (approx.) = x d / D   (since theta is small, sin theta ~ tan theta = x/D).
BRIGHT fringe (maxima):  x d / D = n*lambda  =>  x_n = n*lambda*D / d,  n = 0, 1, 2, ...
DARK fringe (minima):    x d / D = (n + 1/2)*lambda  =>  x_n = (2n + 1)*lambda*D / (2d).
The FRINGE WIDTH beta (the distance between two successive bright, or two successive dark, fringes) is
   beta = lambda D / d.
All fringes are equally spaced and (for monochromatic light) of equal brightness. Note that beta increases with lambda and D, and decreases as the slit separation d increases. With WHITE light the central fringe is white and the others are coloured (violet nearest the centre, red farthest) because beta depends on lambda.

Worked example (YDSE): Two slits 0.2 mm apart are illuminated by light of wavelength 600 nm; the screen is 1.0 m away. Fringe width beta = lambda D / d = (600 x 10^-9 x 1.0) / (0.2 x 10^-3) = 6.0 x 10^-7 / 2 x 10^-4 = 3.0 x 10^-3 m = 3.0 mm.
Worked example (find lambda): If in a YDSE d = 1.0 mm, D = 1.0 m and the measured fringe width is 0.5 mm, then lambda = beta d / D = (0.5 x 10^-3 x 1.0 x 10^-3) / 1.0 = 5.0 x 10^-7 m = 500 nm.

20.8 DIFFRACTION OF LIGHT AT A SINGLE SLIT

DIFFRACTION is the bending of waves around the edges of an obstacle or aperture, and the spreading of light into the geometrical shadow region. It is significant when the aperture size is comparable to the wavelength.
When parallel light of wavelength lambda passes through a single slit of width a and is focused on a screen, we see a broad bright CENTRAL MAXIMUM flanked by alternate dark and (weaker) bright bands. Treating the slit as many secondary Huygens sources, the DARK fringes (minima) occur where the path difference between wavelets from the two edges is a whole number of wavelengths:
   a sin theta = n*lambda,   n = 1, 2, 3, ...   (minima).
The SECONDARY MAXIMA lie approximately at a sin theta = (n + 1/2)*lambda. The central maximum lies between the first minima on either side (n = +/-1). Its angular half-width is sin theta = lambda / a, so the central maximum is TWICE as wide as the other maxima and by far the brightest. The linear width of the central maximum on a screen at distance D (for small angles) is
   width = 2 D lambda / a.
Thus a NARROWER slit (smaller a) gives a WIDER, more spread-out pattern - more diffraction. A wide slit (a >> lambda) gives a sharp bright patch and geometrical optics is recovered.

Worked example (single slit): Light of wavelength 600 nm falls on a slit of width 0.1 mm; the screen is 2.0 m away. Half-angular width of central maximum: sin theta = lambda/a = (600 x 10^-9)/(0.1 x 10^-3) = 6 x 10^-3 rad. Width of central maximum = 2 D lambda / a = 2 x 2.0 x 6 x 10^-3 = 2.4 x 10^-2 m = 24 mm.

20.9 INTERFERENCE VS DIFFRACTION

Both arise from superposition, but they differ:
 - Interference is superposition of waves from TWO (or a few) separate coherent sources; diffraction is superposition of secondary wavelets from DIFFERENT PARTS OF THE SAME wavefront.
 - Interference fringes are (ideally) equally spaced and of equal intensity; diffraction bands are unequally spaced and their intensity falls off rapidly away from the centre.
 - In interference the dark fringes are (nearly) perfectly dark; in diffraction the minima are not perfectly dark and the central maximum is much brighter and wider than the rest.

20.10 RESOLVING POWER (BRIEF)

Diffraction sets a limit on how finely an instrument can distinguish two close objects. By Rayleigh's criterion, two point sources are just resolved when the central maximum of one falls on the first minimum of the other. For a circular aperture of diameter D the smallest resolvable angular separation is theta_min ~ 1.22 lambda / D. The RESOLVING POWER is 1/theta_min; it improves (smaller theta_min) with a LARGER aperture D or a SHORTER wavelength lambda. This is why large telescopes and electron microscopes (very short wavelength) resolve fine detail.

20.11 POLARIZATION OF LIGHT

Light is a TRANSVERSE electromagnetic wave: the electric field vector E oscillates perpendicular to the direction of propagation. In ordinary (unpolarized) light, E vibrates in all directions in the plane perpendicular to propagation, randomly and rapidly. If the vibrations are confined to a SINGLE plane, the light is PLANE-POLARIZED (linearly polarized). The plane containing the vibrations is the plane of vibration.
Only transverse waves can be polarized; longitudinal waves (like sound) cannot. So the fact that light can be polarized is direct proof that light is a transverse wave.
A POLAROID is a sheet that transmits only the component of E along its transmission axis. When unpolarized light of intensity I0 passes through a polaroid, the transmitted intensity is I0/2 and the light is now plane polarized.

MALUS'S LAW: If plane-polarized light of intensity I0 is incident on an analyser (a second polaroid) whose axis makes angle theta with the plane of vibration, the transmitted intensity is
   I = I0 cos^2 theta.
At theta = 0 the analyser passes all the light (I = I0); at theta = 90 degrees it passes none (I = 0, 'crossed' polaroids). Rotating one polaroid makes the field brighten and darken twice per full turn.

POLARIZATION BY REFLECTION - BREWSTER'S LAW: When unpolarized light is reflected from a transparent surface (glass, water), the reflected light is partially polarized, and it is COMPLETELY plane-polarized at one special angle of incidence i_p, the polarizing (Brewster) angle. At this angle the reflected and refracted rays are at right angles to each other, and
   tan i_p = n   (Brewster's law),
where n is the refractive index of the reflecting medium. For glass (n = 1.5), i_p = arctan(1.5) ~ 56 degrees.
APPLICATIONS OF POLAROIDS: polarizing sunglasses (cut glare, which is partly polarized reflected light), photographic filters, LCD displays, stress analysis in transparent models (photoelasticity), controlling light intensity, and 3-D cinema glasses.

Worked example (Malus): Plane-polarized light of intensity I0 falls on an analyser at 60 degrees to its axis. Transmitted intensity I = I0 cos^2 60 = I0 x (0.5)^2 = I0/4.
Worked example (Brewster): The polarizing angle for a glass surface is measured as 57 degrees. Refractive index n = tan 57 ~ 1.54.

SUMMARY

- Light is a wave (an electromagnetic, transverse wave); wave optics explains interference, diffraction and polarization, which ray optics cannot.
- A wavefront is a surface of constant phase; rays are normals to it. Sources give spherical, cylindrical or (at large distance) plane wavefronts.
- Huygens' principle: every point of a wavefront is a source of secondary wavelets; their forward envelope is the new wavefront. It reproduces the laws of reflection and Snell's law of refraction (sin i / sin r = v1/v2 = n2/n1); in a denser medium light slows and its wavelength shortens while frequency is unchanged.
- Sustained interference needs coherent sources (same frequency, constant phase difference). Constructive: path difference = n*lambda; destructive: path difference = (n + 1/2)*lambda.
- Young's double slit: path difference = d sin theta = x d/D; bright at x = n*lambda*D/d; fringe width beta = lambda D / d.
- Single-slit diffraction: broad central maximum with minima at a sin theta = n*lambda; central maximum width = 2 D lambda / a; a narrower slit spreads the pattern more.
- Interference (two sources, equal fringes) differs from diffraction (one wavefront, unequal fringes). Resolving power ~ D / (1.22 lambda) improves with larger aperture and shorter wavelength.
- Polarization confines E to one plane and proves light is transverse. Malus's law: I = I0 cos^2 theta. Brewster's law: tan i_p = n (reflected and refracted rays perpendicular). Polaroids are used in sunglasses, LCDs and glare reduction.

sections.heading: Wavefronts and Huygens' principle
bullets: A wavefront is a surface on which every point vibrates in the same phase; the direction of propagation (a ray) is perpendicular to the wavefront.

Huygens' principle: every point on a wavefront is a source of secondary wavelets spreading forward at the wave speed; after time t the new wavefront is the forward envelope (common tangent) of these wavelets.
The construction correctly predicts the laws of reflection and refraction.

sections.heading: Reflection and refraction from wave theory
bullets: Applying Huygens' construction to a plane wavefront at a plane mirror gives angle of incidence = angle of reflection.

bullets: Interference is the superposition of two coherent waves: crest-on-crest gives a bright fringe, crest-on-trough gives a dark fringe.

sections.heading: Diffraction and resolving power
bullets: Diffraction is the bending of light around edges and into the geometrical shadow, significant when the aperture is comparable to lambda.
A single slit of width a gives a broad central maximum with minima at a sin theta = n*lambda (n = 1, 2, ...).
The central maximum is twice as wide as the others; its linear width is 2D*lambda/a, so a narrower slit spreads the light more.
Resolving power (by Rayleigh's criterion, theta_min ~ 1.22 lambda/D) improves with a larger aperture and a shorter wavelength.

sections.heading: Polarization of light
bullets: Light is a transverse wave; in unpolarized light the electric field vibrates in all perpendicular directions, while in plane-polarized light it is confined to one plane.
Only transverse waves can be polarized, so polarization is direct evidence that light is transverse.
A polaroid transmits only the E-component along its axis; Malus's law gives the transmitted intensity as I = I0 cos^2 theta.
Light reflected at the Brewster angle i_p (tan i_p = n) is completely plane-polarized, with reflected and refracted rays at 90 degrees; polaroids are used in sunglasses, LCDs and glare reduction.

worksheet.title: Worksheet - Wave Phenomena and Light (Wave Optics)
worksheet.instructions: Attempt all questions. Show your working for numerical problems. Take the speed of light c = 3 x 10^8 m/s and use lambda = 600 nm where a wavelength is not specified. Answers should use plain-text notation (lambda, theta, cos^2, sqrt).

questions.question: State Huygens' principle and explain how it is used to construct a new wavefront from an old one.
questions.answer:
Huygens' principle has two parts: (1) every point on a given wavefront acts as a fresh source of secondary wavelets that spread forward with the wave speed v of the medium; (2) after a time t, the new position of the wavefront is the surface tangent to all these secondary wavelets (the forward envelope).
Construction: from each point of the old wavefront draw a sphere (a circle in 2-D) of radius v*t. Draw the common tangent to all these spheres on the forward side. This tangent surface is the new wavefront. The backward tangent is discarded because no back-travelling wave is observed.
questions.explanation: Two-part statement plus the envelope construction using radius v*t.

questions.question: Distinguish between a spherical wavefront and a plane wavefront, and state how a plane wavefront can be obtained from a point source.
questions.answer: A SPHERICAL wavefront is a set of concentric spheres produced by a point source in a uniform medium; the rays are radial (diverging). A PLANE wavefront is flat and its rays are parallel. A plane wavefront is obtained from a point source by placing the source at the focus of a converging lens (or a concave mirror), or simply by going very far from the source, because a small portion of a very large sphere is almost flat.
questions.explanation: Shape and rays; plane wavefront via lens/large distance.

questions.question: Using Huygens' principle, obtain Snell's law of refraction and state what happens to the speed, wavelength and frequency of light when it enters a denser medium.
questions.answer:
Let a plane wavefront AB in medium 1 (speed v1) meet the boundary XY and enter medium 2 (speed v2). While the wavelet from B travels BB' = v1*t to reach the surface at B', the wavelet from A enters medium 2 and travels AA' = v2*t. The refracted wavefront is A'B'.
In triangle ABB': sin i = BB'/AB' = v1*t/AB'. In triangle AA'B': sin r = AA'/AB' = v2*t/AB'.
Dividing: sin i / sin r = v1/v2 = constant. Writing v1 = c/n1 and v2 = c/n2 gives sin i/sin r = n2/n1, which is Snell's law, and n1 sin i = n2 sin r.
On entering a denser medium (v2 < v1): SPEED decreases; WAVELENGTH decreases (lambda_medium = lambda_vacuum/n) because lambda = v/f and f is fixed; FREQUENCY is UNCHANGED (it is set by the source). The ray bends toward the normal.
questions.explanation: Geometry of the two triangles gives sin i/sin r = v1/v2 = n2/n1; speed and lambda fall, f constant.

questions.question: What are coherent sources? Why can two independent light bulbs not produce a sustained interference pattern?
questions.answer: Coherent sources are two sources that emit waves of the SAME frequency (and wavelength) with a CONSTANT phase difference that does not change with time. Two independent bulbs are incoherent: each atom emits light in short bursts lasting about 10^-8 s, so the phase of each source fluctuates randomly and independently. The phase difference between the two bulbs therefore changes millions of times per second, and the bright/dark pattern shifts too fast to be seen - the eye records only uniform illumination. Coherent sources are instead obtained by deriving both from a single source (as with the two slits in Young's experiment).
questions.explanation: Definition (same f, constant phase diff) + random phase of independent sources.

questions.question: In a Young's double-slit experiment the slits are 0.5 mm apart and the screen is 1.5 m away. Light of wavelength 600 nm is used. Calculate the fringe width and the distance of the 3rd bright fringe from the centre.
questions.answer:
Given d = 0.5 mm = 5 x 10^-4 m, D = 1.5 m, lambda = 600 nm = 6 x 10^-7 m.
Fringe width beta = lambda D / d = (6 x 10^-7 x 1.5) / (5 x 10^-4) = (9 x 10^-7)/(5 x 10^-4) = 1.8 x 10^-3 m = 1.8 mm.
The n-th bright fringe is at x_n = n*beta. For n = 3: x_3 = 3 x 1.8 mm = 5.4 mm from the centre.
questions.explanation: beta = lambda D/d = 1.8 mm; x_3 = 3 beta = 5.4 mm.

questions.question: In a double-slit experiment, the fringe width is 0.4 mm when the screen is 1.0 m from the slits. Find the new fringe width if the screen is moved to 1.5 m (all else unchanged).
questions.answer:
Fringe width beta = lambda D / d, so for fixed lambda and d, beta is proportional to D.
beta1/D1 = beta2/D2  =>  beta2 = beta1 x (D2/D1) = 0.4 mm x (1.5/1.0) = 0.6 mm.
The fringe width increases to 0.6 mm.
questions.explanation: beta proportional to D; beta2 = 0.4 x 1.5 = 0.6 mm.

questions.question: Monochromatic light of wavelength 500 nm falls normally on a single slit of width 0.25 mm. The pattern is observed on a screen 1.0 m away. Find the width of the central maximum.
questions.answer:
Given lambda = 500 nm = 5 x 10^-7 m, a = 0.25 mm = 2.5 x 10^-4 m, D = 1.0 m.
The first minima on either side occur at sin theta = lambda/a. The width of the central maximum (between the two first minima) is
width = 2 D lambda / a = (2 x 1.0 x 5 x 10^-7)/(2.5 x 10^-4) = (1.0 x 10^-6)/(2.5 x 10^-4) = 4.0 x 10^-3 m = 4.0 mm.
questions.explanation: Central maximum width = 2 D lambda / a = 4.0 mm.

questions.question: State two differences between interference and diffraction of light.
questions.answer:
(1) Interference is the superposition of waves from TWO (or a few) separate coherent sources, whereas diffraction is the superposition of secondary wavelets from DIFFERENT PARTS OF THE SAME wavefront.
(2) In interference, all bright fringes are (ideally) equally spaced and of equal intensity, and the dark fringes are perfectly dark; in diffraction, the bands are unequally spaced, the intensity of the maxima falls off rapidly away from the centre, and the central maximum is much wider and brighter than the rest.
questions.explanation: Source (two vs same wavefront) and fringe spacing/intensity.

questions.question: Plane-polarized light of intensity I0 is incident on an analyser. Find the transmitted intensity when the angle between the light's plane of vibration and the analyser axis is (a) 0 degrees, (b) 30 degrees, (c) 90 degrees.
questions.answer:
By Malus's law, I = I0 cos^2 theta.
(a) theta = 0: I = I0 cos^2 0 = I0 x 1 = I0.
(b) theta = 30: cos 30 = 0.866, cos^2 30 = 0.75, so I = 0.75 I0 = (3/4) I0.
(c) theta = 90: cos 90 = 0, so I = 0 (no light passes - crossed polaroids).
questions.explanation: Malus's law: I0, (3/4)I0, 0.

questions.question: (a) State Brewster's law. (b) Light is reflected from a glass surface of refractive index 1.5. Find the polarizing angle. (c) What is the angle between the reflected and refracted rays at this angle, and what is the state of polarization of the reflected ray?
questions.answer:
(a) Brewster's law: when unpolarized light is reflected from a transparent surface, the reflected ray is completely plane-polarized at one angle of incidence i_p (the polarizing/Brewster angle), and tan i_p = n, where n is the refractive index of the surface.
(b) tan i_p = n = 1.5, so i_p = arctan(1.5) = 56.3 degrees (about 56 degrees).
(c) At the polarizing angle the reflected and refracted rays are perpendicular, i.e. the angle between them is 90 degrees. The reflected ray is completely plane-polarized (its vibrations are perpendicular to the plane of incidence).
questions.explanation: Brewster's law statement; i_p = arctan 1.5 ~ 56 deg; reflected-refracted at 90 deg; reflected ray fully polarized.

questions.question: Define a wavefront and state the relation between a wavefront and a ray.
questions.answer: A wavefront is a surface on which all points vibrate in the same phase (the locus of points reached by the disturbance at the same instant). A ray is a line drawn perpendicular (normal) to the wavefront and represents the direction in which the wave travels. Thus rays and wavefronts are always mutually perpendicular.
questions.explanation: Model answer for a NIOS wave-optics short-answer question; see the answer for the reasoning and formulae used.

questions.question: Name the type of wavefront produced by (a) a point source, (b) a line source, (c) a source at infinity.
questions.answer: (a) A point source produces SPHERICAL wavefronts (concentric spheres). (b) A line source produces CYLINDRICAL wavefronts. (c) A source at infinity (or very far away) produces a PLANE wavefront, for which the rays are parallel.
questions.explanation: Model answer for a NIOS wave-optics short-answer question; see the answer for the reasoning and formulae used.

questions.question: State the two parts of Huygens' principle and describe how the new wavefront is obtained.
questions.answer: (1) Every point on a wavefront is a fresh source of secondary wavelets that travel forward with the speed v of the wave in the medium. (2) After a time t, the new wavefront is the surface that touches (is tangent to) all these secondary wavelets on the forward side. To find it, draw a sphere of radius v*t about each point of the old wavefront and take the forward common tangent (envelope); that envelope is the new wavefront.
questions.explanation: Model answer for a NIOS wave-optics short-answer question; see the answer for the reasoning and formulae used.

questions.question: Using Huygens' principle, show that the angle of incidence equals the angle of reflection at a plane mirror.
questions.answer: Let a plane wavefront AB strike a plane mirror. Point A reaches the mirror first and emits a secondary wavelet into the same medium (speed v). By the time the other edge B reaches the surface at B' (time t, BB' = v*t), the wavelet from A has radius AA' = v*t. Drawing the tangent from B' to this wavelet gives the reflected wavefront A'B'. Triangles ABB' and B'A'A are congruent (right angles at B and A', common hypotenuse AB', AA' = BB'). Hence the angle of incidence i = angle of reflection r, and the incident ray, reflected ray and normal lie in one plane.
questions.explanation: Model answer for a NIOS wave-optics short-answer question; see the answer for the reasoning and formulae used.

questions.question: When light passes from air into water, state what happens to its speed, wavelength and frequency.
questions.answer: Water is optically denser than air (n_water > n_air). So the SPEED of light decreases (v = c/n). The WAVELENGTH decreases (lambda_medium = lambda_vacuum/n). The FREQUENCY remains UNCHANGED, because it is determined by the source and does not change on crossing a boundary.
questions.explanation: Model answer for a NIOS wave-optics short-answer question; see the answer for the reasoning and formulae used.

questions.question: Light travels from medium 1 into medium 2. The angle of incidence is 45 degrees and the angle of refraction is 30 degrees. Find (a) the ratio of speeds v1/v2 and (b) the refractive index of medium 2 relative to medium 1.
questions.answer:
By Huygens' derivation, sin i/sin r = v1/v2 = n2/n1 (relative refractive index).
(a) v1/v2 = sin 45/sin 30 = (0.707)/(0.5) = 1.414 (about sqrt 2).
(b) The refractive index of medium 2 relative to medium 1 is n21 = sin i/sin r = 1.414. So medium 2 is denser; light slows by a factor of about 1.414 on entering it.
questions.explanation: Model answer for a NIOS wave-optics short-answer question; see the answer for the reasoning and formulae used.

questions.question: What are coherent sources? Give one way of producing them.
questions.answer: Coherent sources are two sources that emit waves of the same frequency (and wavelength) with a constant phase difference that does not vary with time. They are produced by deriving two sources from a SINGLE original source - for example, the two slits in Young's double-slit experiment, both illuminated by the same wavefront, or by division of amplitude in thin films.
questions.explanation: Model answer for a NIOS wave-optics short-answer question; see the answer for the reasoning and formulae used.

questions.question: State the conditions required to obtain a steady (sustained) and clearly visible interference pattern.
questions.answer: For a sustained, visible interference pattern: (1) the two sources must be COHERENT - same frequency and a constant phase difference; (2) they should emit light of the SAME wavelength (monochromatic) for sharp fringes; (3) the two beams should have nearly EQUAL AMPLITUDES so that dark fringes are truly dark and contrast is good; (4) the sources should be NARROW and CLOSE together, and (for unpolarized light) in the same state of polarization. If these hold, bright and dark fringes remain fixed and clear.
questions.explanation: Model answer for a NIOS wave-optics short-answer question; see the answer for the reasoning and formulae used.

questions.question: Write the conditions on path difference for (a) bright and (b) dark fringes, and the corresponding phase differences.
questions.answer: (a) BRIGHT (constructive): path difference = n*lambda (n = 0, 1, 2, ...); phase difference = 2n*pi (even multiples of pi). (b) DARK (destructive): path difference = (n + 1/2)*lambda = (2n-1)*lambda/2; phase difference = (2n-1)*pi (odd multiples of pi).

questions.question: In a Young's double-slit experiment, d = 0.8 mm, D = 1.2 m and lambda = 480 nm. Find (a) the fringe width and (b) the distance between the 2nd and 5th bright fringes.
questions.answer:
Given d = 8 x 10^-4 m, D = 1.2 m, lambda = 4.8 x 10^-7 m.
(a) beta = lambda D/d = (4.8e-7 x 1.2)/(8e-4) = (5.76e-7)/(8e-4) = 7.2 x 10^-4 m = 0.72 mm.
(b) Successive bright fringes are separated by beta. From the 2nd to the 5th there are (5 - 2) = 3 fringe widths: distance = 3 x 0.72 mm = 2.16 mm.

questions.question: In a YDSE the fringe width is 1.0 mm. What will be the new fringe width if the slit separation is doubled and everything else is kept the same?
questions.answer: Fringe width beta = lambda D/d is inversely proportional to d. Doubling d halves beta. So the new fringe width = 1.0 mm / 2 = 0.5 mm.

questions.question: A double-slit is illuminated by light of wavelength 600 nm and the fringe width is 1.2 mm. If the same setup is used with light of wavelength 400 nm, find the new fringe width and the ratio of the two fringe widths.
questions.answer:
Fringe width beta = lambda D/d is proportional to lambda (D and d fixed).
beta1/lambda1 = beta2/lambda2 => beta2 = beta1 x (lambda2/lambda1) = 1.2 mm x (400/600) = 1.2 x (2/3) = 0.8 mm.
Ratio beta1:beta2 = 600:400 = 3:2. So with 400 nm light the fringes are narrower (0.8 mm).

questions.question: What is diffraction of light? When is it easily observed?
questions.answer: Diffraction is the bending of light waves around the edges of an obstacle or aperture and the spreading of light into the region of the geometrical shadow. It is easily observed when the size of the obstacle or aperture is COMPARABLE to the wavelength of light. Because visible-light wavelengths are very small (~10^-7 m), pronounced diffraction requires very narrow slits or fine structures.

questions.question: Monochromatic light of wavelength 500 nm is incident on a single slit of width 0.1 mm. The screen is 1.0 m away. Find (a) the angular position of the first minimum and (b) the width of the central maximum.
questions.answer:
Given lambda = 5 x 10^-7 m, a = 1 x 10^-4 m, D = 1.0 m.
(a) First minimum: a sin theta = lambda, so sin theta = lambda/a = 5e-7/1e-4 = 5 x 10^-3 rad (about 0.29 degrees).
(b) Width of central maximum = 2 D lambda/a = 2 x 1.0 x 5e-7/1e-4 = 1.0 x 10^-2 m = 10 mm.

questions.question: How does the width of the central maximum in single-slit diffraction change if (a) the slit is made narrower, (b) a longer wavelength is used?
questions.answer: The width of the central maximum is 2D*lambda/a. (a) Making the slit NARROWER (smaller a) INCREASES the width - the pattern spreads out more. (b) Using a LONGER wavelength (larger lambda) also INCREASES the width. Both changes make diffraction more pronounced.

questions.question: In a single-slit diffraction experiment, the first minimum for light of wavelength 600 nm is observed at an angle of 30 degrees. Find the width of the slit.
questions.answer: First minimum: a sin theta = lambda (n = 1). So a = lambda/sin theta = (600 x 10^-9)/sin 30 = (6 x 10^-7)/(0.5) = 1.2 x 10^-6 m = 1.2 micrometre. The slit is very narrow (about twice the wavelength), which is why the first minimum is at as large an angle as 30 degrees.

questions.question: Give three points of difference between interference and diffraction of light.
questions.answer:
(1) SOURCE: Interference is superposition of waves from two (or a few) separate coherent sources; diffraction is superposition of secondary wavelets from different parts of the same wavefront.
(2) FRINGE SPACING/INTENSITY: Interference fringes are equally spaced and (ideally) of equal intensity; diffraction bands are unequally spaced and the intensity of the maxima falls off rapidly from the centre.
(3) DARK FRINGES: In interference the dark fringes are perfectly dark; in diffraction the minima are not perfectly dark, and the central maximum is much brighter and wider than the others.

questions.question: What is meant by the resolving power of an optical instrument? State the two factors that improve it.
questions.answer: The resolving power of an optical instrument is its ability to form separate (distinguishable) images of two objects that are very close together. By Rayleigh's criterion the smallest resolvable angle is theta_min ~ 1.22 lambda/D, so resolving power (= 1/theta_min) is improved by (1) using a LARGER aperture diameter D, and (2) using a SHORTER wavelength lambda.
questions.explanation: Model answer for a NIOS wave-optics short-answer question; see the answer for the reasoning and formulae used.

questions.question: What is plane-polarized light, and why can it not be produced from sound waves?
questions.answer: Plane-polarized (linearly polarized) light is light in which the electric-field vibrations are confined to a single plane perpendicular to the direction of propagation, instead of vibrating in all directions. Sound waves are LONGITUDINAL - the particles vibrate along the direction of propagation, so there is no transverse vibration to restrict to a plane. Therefore sound cannot be polarized; polarization is a property of transverse waves only.
questions.explanation: Model answer for a NIOS wave-optics short-answer question; see the answer for the reasoning and formulae used.

questions.question: Explain how the phenomenon of polarization establishes the transverse nature of light. Mention one application of polaroids.
questions.answer: Polarization means the vibrations of a wave can be confined to a single plane. This is only possible if the vibrations are PERPENDICULAR to the direction of travel - i.e. the wave is TRANSVERSE. A longitudinal wave (vibration along the direction of travel) has no sideways vibration to confine, so it cannot be polarized. Since light CAN be polarized (e.g. by a polaroid, or on reflection), light must be a transverse wave. Application: polarizing sunglasses cut glare (reflected polarized light); other uses include LCD screens, photographic filters and 3-D cinema glasses.

questions.question: State Malus's law. Plane-polarized light of intensity I0 passes through an analyser oriented at 45 degrees. Find the transmitted intensity.
questions.answer: Malus's law: when plane-polarized light of intensity I0 falls on an analyser whose axis makes angle theta with the plane of vibration, the transmitted intensity is I = I0 cos^2 theta. At theta = 45 degrees: cos 45 = 1/sqrt 2, so cos^2 45 = 1/2. Therefore I = I0/2.

questions.question: State Brewster's law. The polarizing angle for a certain glass is 58 degrees. Find its refractive index and the angle of refraction at that incidence.
questions.answer: Brewster's law: at the polarizing angle i_p the reflected light is completely plane-polarized and tan i_p = n. Here i_p = 58 degrees, so n = tan 58 = 1.60. At the Brewster angle the reflected and refracted rays are perpendicular, so the angle of refraction r = 90 - i_p = 90 - 58 = 32 degrees. (Check: tan 58 = sin 58/cos 58, and n = sin i_p/sin r = sin 58/sin 32 = 0.848/0.530 = 1.60, consistent.)
questions.explanation: Model answer for a NIOS wave-optics short-answer question; see the answer for the reasoning and formulae used.

questions.question: Using Huygens' principle, derive Snell's law of refraction. State clearly what happens to the frequency and wavelength of light as it goes from a rarer to a denser medium.
questions.answer:
Consider a plane wavefront AB travelling in medium 1 (speed v1) and meeting the plane boundary XY separating it from a denser medium 2 (speed v2). Let the wavefront reach A on the boundary first. While the wavelet from B travels the distance BB' = v1*t to reach the surface at B', the wavelet starting from A enters medium 2 and travels a smaller distance AA' = v2*t (because v2 < v1). The refracted wavefront is the tangent A'B'.
Let i be the angle of incidence and r the angle of refraction. In right triangle ABB', sin i = BB'/AB' = v1*t/AB'. In right triangle AA'B', sin r = AA'/AB' = v2*t/AB'. Dividing,
   sin i/sin r = v1/v2 = constant.
Since v = c/n, v1/v2 = n2/n1, giving Snell's law n1 sin i = n2 sin r.
Going from a rarer to a denser medium: the FREQUENCY is UNCHANGED (fixed by the source). The SPEED decreases (v2 < v1) and, because lambda = v/f, the WAVELENGTH also DECREASES (lambda2 = lambda1 x v2/v1 = lambda1/n21). The ray bends toward the normal.

questions.question: Describe Young's double-slit experiment. Derive the expression for fringe width and the positions of bright and dark fringes.
questions.answer:
SETUP: Light from a single narrow slit S falls on two close parallel slits S1 and S2 (separation d). Because both slits receive light from the same wavefront, they act as COHERENT sources. Their overlapping waves fall on a screen a distance D away, producing alternate bright and dark fringes.
PATH DIFFERENCE: Consider a point P at distance x from the centre O. The path difference is S2P - S1P. For d << D and small angle theta, this equals d sin theta ~ d tan theta = x d/D.
BRIGHT FRINGES (constructive): path difference = n*lambda => x d/D = n*lambda => x_n = n*lambda*D/d, n = 0, 1, 2, ...
DARK FRINGES (destructive): path difference = (n + 1/2)*lambda => x_n = (2n+1)*lambda*D/(2d).
FRINGE WIDTH: the spacing between consecutive bright fringes is
   beta = x_(n+1) - x_n = (n+1)*lambda*D/d - n*lambda*D/d = lambda*D/d.
Thus beta = lambda D/d. Fringes are equally spaced; beta increases with lambda and D and decreases as d increases. With white light the central fringe is white and the neighbouring fringes are coloured.

questions.question: Describe the diffraction of light at a single slit. Obtain the condition for the minima and an expression for the width of the central maximum.
questions.answer:
When parallel monochromatic light of wavelength lambda falls normally on a single slit of width a and is collected by a lens on a screen, a broad bright CENTRAL MAXIMUM appears, flanked by alternate dark and (weaker) bright bands.
Treat the slit as a large number of secondary Huygens sources across its width a. Consider light diffracted at angle theta. The path difference between wavelets from the two edges of the slit is a sin theta. Divide the slit into two halves: if the path difference between the edges is lambda, then each point in the upper half has a partner in the lower half exactly lambda/2 out of phase, so all contributions cancel in pairs - giving a MINIMUM. In general,
   a sin theta = n*lambda,  n = 1, 2, 3, ...  (dark fringes / minima).
The SECONDARY MAXIMA lie roughly midway, at a sin theta = (n + 1/2)*lambda.
CENTRAL MAXIMUM: it lies between the first minima on either side (n = +/-1), at sin theta = +/- lambda/a. For small angles theta ~ lambda/a, so on a screen at distance D the half-width is D*lambda/a and the full width is
   width = 2 D lambda/a.
The central maximum is thus twice as wide as the other bands and is the brightest. A narrower slit (smaller a) gives a wider, more spread-out pattern; a very wide slit gives a sharp bright patch (ray optics).

questions.question: Explain the phenomenon of interference of light using the superposition principle. Distinguish constructive from destructive interference and explain why energy is conserved.
questions.answer:
INTERFERENCE arises when two coherent waves overlap. By the SUPERPOSITION PRINCIPLE, the resultant displacement at any point is the algebraic sum of the displacements due to the individual waves.
CONSTRUCTIVE interference: where the two waves arrive IN PHASE (crest on crest, trough on trough), they reinforce. The path difference is n*lambda (phase difference 2n*pi), amplitudes add, and a BRIGHT fringe of maximum intensity results (intensity ~ (a1 + a2)^2).
DESTRUCTIVE interference: where the waves arrive OUT OF PHASE by half a cycle (crest on trough), they cancel. The path difference is (n + 1/2)*lambda (phase difference (2n-1)*pi), amplitudes subtract, and a DARK fringe of minimum intensity results (intensity ~ (a1 - a2)^2; zero if a1 = a2).
ENERGY CONSERVATION: interference does not create or destroy energy - it only REDISTRIBUTES it. The energy that is 'missing' from the dark fringes is not lost; it is added to the bright fringes, whose intensity exceeds the sum of the two separate intensities by just the right amount. Averaged over the whole pattern, the total energy equals the sum of the energies of the two beams.

questions.question: State Malus's law and Brewster's law. (a) Unpolarized light of intensity I0 passes through two polaroids whose axes are at 30 degrees. Find the final intensity. (b) Find the polarizing angle for water (n = 1.33).
questions.answer:
MALUS'S LAW: For plane-polarized light of intensity I incident on an analyser at angle theta to its axis, transmitted intensity = I cos^2 theta.
BREWSTER'S LAW: The reflected light is completely plane-polarized at the polarizing angle i_p, where tan i_p = n (refractive index), and the reflected and refracted rays are then perpendicular.
(a) The first polaroid transmits half of the unpolarized light: I1 = I0/2, now plane-polarized along the first axis. The second polaroid is at 30 degrees, so by Malus's law I2 = I1 cos^2 30 = (I0/2) x (0.866)^2 = (I0/2) x 0.75 = 0.375 I0 = 3 I0/8.
(b) tan i_p = n = 1.33, so i_p = arctan(1.33) = 53.1 degrees (about 53 degrees). This is why polarizing sunglasses are effective against glare reflected from water at around this angle.
questions.explanation: Model long answer for a NIOS wave-optics question; the answer gives the full derivation/explanation and worked steps expected.

questions.question: What is a wavefront? Describe the different types of wavefronts with the shape of the corresponding rays, and state Huygens' principle.
questions.answer:
A WAVEFRONT is a surface on which every point vibrates in the same phase - the locus of all points that the disturbance reaches at the same instant. The direction of propagation (the RAY) is always perpendicular (normal) to the wavefront.
TYPES:
(1) SPHERICAL wavefront - produced by a point source in a uniform medium; the wavefronts are concentric spheres and the rays are radial (diverging outward).
(2) CYLINDRICAL wavefront - produced by a line (slit) source; the wavefronts are coaxial cylinders.
(3) PLANE wavefront - produced by a source at a great distance (or at the focus of a lens); the wavefront is flat and the rays are parallel.
HUYGENS' PRINCIPLE: (i) every point on a wavefront is a source of secondary wavelets spreading forward at the wave speed v; (ii) after time t, the new wavefront is the forward common tangent (envelope) of all these wavelets, each of radius v*t. This construction predicts how wavefronts advance and explains reflection and refraction.

questions.question: Compare interference and diffraction of light in detail, and explain what is meant by the resolving power of a telescope and how it can be increased.
questions.answer:
INTERFERENCE vs DIFFRACTION:
- Origin: interference is superposition of waves from TWO separate coherent sources; diffraction is superposition of secondary wavelets from DIFFERENT PARTS of the SAME wavefront.
- Fringe width: interference fringes are equally spaced; diffraction bands are unequally spaced (the central band is widest).
- Intensity: interference maxima are (ideally) all equally bright; diffraction maxima decrease rapidly in brightness away from the centre.
- Dark fringes: interference minima are perfectly dark; diffraction minima are not perfectly dark.
RESOLVING POWER of a telescope is its ability to form separate images of two distant objects (e.g. two close stars) that subtend a very small angle. Because of diffraction at the objective aperture, each star's image is a small diffraction disc. By RAYLEIGH'S CRITERION two objects are just resolved when the central maximum of one falls on the first minimum of the other, giving a minimum resolvable angle theta_min = 1.22 lambda/D, where D is the aperture diameter. The resolving power (1/theta_min = D/(1.22 lambda)) is INCREASED by using a LARGER objective aperture D and/or a SHORTER wavelength lambda. This is why large telescopes gather more detail.
questions.explanation: Model long answer for a NIOS wave-optics question; the answer gives the full derivation/explanation and worked steps expected.

questions.question: Explain what is meant by unpolarized and plane-polarized light. Describe how a polaroid produces plane-polarized light and how a second polaroid (analyser) can be used to detect it. What happens as the analyser is rotated?
questions.answer:
UNPOLARIZED LIGHT: ordinary light in which the electric-field vector vibrates in all directions in the plane perpendicular to the direction of propagation, changing randomly and very rapidly. No single vibration plane is preferred.
PLANE-POLARIZED LIGHT: light in which the electric-field vibrations are confined to a SINGLE plane perpendicular to the direction of propagation.
POLAROID AS POLARIZER: a polaroid sheet has a transmission axis and passes only the component of the electric field parallel to that axis, absorbing the perpendicular component. So unpolarized light of intensity I0 emerges with intensity I0/2 and is now plane-polarized along the axis.
ANALYSER: a second polaroid placed in the beam is used to detect polarization. By Malus's law the intensity it transmits is I = (I0/2) cos^2 theta, where theta is the angle between the two axes. As the analyser is ROTATED, the transmitted intensity varies between a MAXIMUM (theta = 0, axes parallel) and ZERO (theta = 90 degrees, 'crossed' polaroids), passing through two maxima and two minima in a full 360-degree rotation. This variation proves the light is plane-polarized (unpolarized light would show no such variation).

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the questions.

Huygens' principle treats every point of a wavefront as a source of secondary wavelets. When a plane wavefront in air (speed v1) meets the surface of glass (speed v2, with v2 < v1), the part of the wavefront that has entered the glass slows down while the rest is still in air. Applying the envelope construction leads to Snell's law.

(i) State the two parts of Huygens' principle.
(ii) Write Snell's law in terms of the speeds v1 and v2.
(iii) State what happens to the wavelength and frequency of the light in the glass.
(iv) For air-to-glass with i = 60 degrees and r = 35 degrees, estimate v1/v2.
questions.answer:
(i) (a) Every point on a wavefront is a source of secondary wavelets spreading forward at the wave speed; (b) after time t the new wavefront is the forward tangent (envelope) of these wavelets.
(ii) sin i/sin r = v1/v2 (= n2/n1).
(iii) In the denser glass the wavelength DECREASES (lambda_glass = lambda_air/n) and the speed decreases, but the frequency is UNCHANGED.
(iv) v1/v2 = sin 60/sin 35 = 0.866/0.574 = 1.51. (This equals the refractive index of the glass, about 1.5.)
questions.explanation: Huygens' two parts; Snell's law v1/v2; lambda down, f constant; ratio ~1.5.

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the questions.

In a Young's double-slit experiment, two slits 0.6 mm apart are illuminated by monochromatic light of wavelength 600 nm. A screen is placed 1.5 m from the slits. Bright and dark fringes are observed.

(i) Why do the two slits behave as coherent sources?
(ii) Calculate the fringe width.
(iii) Find the distance of the 4th bright fringe from the central fringe.
(iv) What change occurs in the fringe width if the wavelength is reduced to 400 nm?
questions.answer:
(i) Both slits are illuminated by the SAME wavefront from a single source, so they always maintain a constant phase difference - they are coherent.
(ii) beta = lambda D/d = (600e-9 x 1.5)/(0.6e-3) = (9e-7)/(6e-4) = 1.5 x 10^-3 m = 1.5 mm.
(iii) 4th bright fringe: x_4 = 4 beta = 4 x 1.5 mm = 6.0 mm.
(iv) beta is proportional to lambda, so reducing lambda from 600 to 400 nm reduces beta to 1.5 x (400/600) = 1.0 mm - the fringes get narrower.
questions.explanation: Coherence from one source; beta = 1.5 mm; x_4 = 6 mm; beta decreases to 1.0 mm.

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the questions.

A single slit of width 0.2 mm is illuminated normally by monochromatic light of wavelength 600 nm. A diffraction pattern is observed on a screen 1.0 m from the slit.

(i) Write the condition for minima in single-slit diffraction.
(ii) Find the angular position of the first minimum.
(iii) Find the width of the central maximum on the screen.
(iv) How would the pattern change if the slit were made narrower?
questions.answer:
(i) Minima occur where a sin theta = n*lambda, with n = 1, 2, 3, ...
(ii) First minimum (n = 1): sin theta = lambda/a = (600e-9)/(0.2e-3) = 3 x 10^-3 rad (about 0.17 degrees).
(iii) Width of central maximum = 2 D lambda/a = 2 x 1.0 x (600e-9)/(0.2e-3) = 6.0 x 10^-3 m = 6.0 mm.
(iv) A narrower slit (smaller a) makes sin theta = lambda/a larger, so the central maximum and the whole pattern SPREAD OUT more - diffraction becomes more pronounced.
questions.explanation: Minima a sin theta = n*lambda; theta1 = 3e-3 rad; width = 6 mm; narrower slit spreads pattern.

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the questions.

Malus's law describes how the intensity of plane-polarized light changes after passing through an analyser: I = I0 cos^2 theta. Brewster's law, tan i_p = n, gives the angle at which reflected light is completely polarized.

(i) Plane-polarized light of intensity I0 passes through an analyser at 0, 45 and 60 degrees. Find the transmitted intensity in each case.
(ii) State Brewster's law.
(iii) Find the polarizing angle for glass of refractive index 1.5.
(iv) At the polarizing angle, what is the angle between the reflected and refracted rays?
questions.answer:
(i) By Malus's law: at 0 deg, I = I0 cos^2 0 = I0. At 45 deg, I = I0 cos^2 45 = I0 x 1/2 = I0/2. At 60 deg, I = I0 cos^2 60 = I0 x 1/4 = I0/4.
(ii) When unpolarized light is reflected at the polarizing angle i_p, the reflected ray is completely plane-polarized and tan i_p = n.
(iii) tan i_p = 1.5, so i_p = arctan 1.5 = 56.3 degrees (about 56 degrees).
(iv) The reflected and refracted rays are at 90 degrees (perpendicular) to each other.
questions.explanation: Malus: I0, I0/2, I0/4; Brewster statement; i_p ~ 56 deg; rays at 90 deg.

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the questions.

A wavefront is a surface of constant phase. Depending on the source and the distance, wavefronts may be spherical, cylindrical or plane. Huygens' principle allows one to construct the next position of a wavefront from the present one.

(i) Define a wavefront and a ray.
(ii) What kind of wavefront does a point source produce nearby, and what kind does it produce very far away?
(iii) State Huygens' principle.
(iv) What is the radius of each secondary wavelet after time t?
questions.answer:
(i) A wavefront is a surface on which all points vibrate in the same phase. A ray is a line drawn perpendicular to the wavefront, showing the direction of propagation.
(ii) Near a point source the wavefronts are SPHERICAL; very far away a small portion is essentially PLANE (flat), with parallel rays.
(iii) Every point on a wavefront acts as a source of secondary wavelets that travel forward at the wave speed; the new wavefront is the forward tangent (envelope) of these wavelets after time t.
(iv) Each secondary wavelet has radius v*t, where v is the wave speed and t is the time.
questions.explanation: Definitions; spherical near / plane far; Huygens' statement; radius v*t.

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the questions.

Interference of light requires two coherent sources. When two coherent waves overlap, bright fringes form where they are in phase and dark fringes where they are out of phase. Two independent bulbs cannot produce a steady pattern.

(i) What are coherent sources?
(ii) Give the path-difference condition for a bright and for a dark fringe.
(iii) Why can two independent bulbs not give a sustained pattern?
(iv) Is energy conserved in interference? Explain briefly.
questions.answer:
(i) Coherent sources emit waves of the same frequency with a constant phase difference that does not change with time.
(ii) Bright (constructive): path difference = n*lambda. Dark (destructive): path difference = (n + 1/2)*lambda.
(iii) Each independent bulb changes its phase randomly about every 10^-8 s, so the phase difference between the two bulbs varies rapidly and randomly; the pattern shifts too fast to be seen, giving uniform illumination.
(iv) Yes. Interference only REDISTRIBUTES energy - the energy absent from the dark fringes reappears in the bright fringes, so the total energy is conserved.
questions.explanation: Coherence; n*lambda and (n+1/2)*lambda; random phase; energy redistributed.

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the questions.

Interference and diffraction both result from superposition of waves, yet their patterns differ. Diffraction also limits the resolving power of instruments such as telescopes and microscopes, described by Rayleigh's criterion.

(i) State one difference in the SOURCE of the waves for interference and diffraction.
(ii) State one difference in the fringe intensity/spacing of the two patterns.
(iii) State Rayleigh's criterion.
(iv) How can the resolving power of a telescope be increased?
questions.answer:
(i) Interference uses waves from TWO separate coherent sources; diffraction uses secondary wavelets from DIFFERENT PARTS of the SAME wavefront.
(ii) Interference fringes are equally spaced and equally bright; diffraction bands are unequally spaced and their brightness falls off rapidly from the centre (and the central band is widest).
(iii) Two point sources are just resolved when the central maximum of the diffraction pattern of one falls on the first minimum of the other.
(iv) By using a LARGER aperture (objective) diameter and/or a SHORTER wavelength, since theta_min = 1.22 lambda/D.
questions.explanation: Source difference; spacing/intensity difference; Rayleigh's criterion; larger D or shorter lambda.

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the questions.

Light is a transverse electromagnetic wave, so it can be polarized. A polaroid transmits only the component of the electric field along its axis. Polaroids are used in sunglasses and LCD screens.

(i) What is plane-polarized light?
(ii) How does polarization prove that light is transverse?
(iii) When unpolarized light of intensity I0 passes through one ideal polaroid, what is the transmitted intensity?
(iv) Give two practical applications of polaroids.
questions.answer:
(i) Plane-polarized light is light whose electric-field vibrations are confined to a single plane perpendicular to the direction of propagation.
(ii) Only transverse waves (vibrations perpendicular to travel) can have their vibrations restricted to one plane. Longitudinal waves cannot be polarized. Since light can be polarized, it must be transverse.
(iii) Half the incident intensity, i.e. I0/2 (and the emerging light is plane-polarized).
(iv) Any two of: polarizing sunglasses (reduce glare), LCD displays, photographic filters, 3-D cinema glasses, stress analysis (photoelasticity), controlling light intensity.
questions.explanation: Definition; transverse proof; I0/2; two applications.

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the questions.

In a Young's double-slit experiment with light of wavelength 500 nm, the fringe width is found to be 1.0 mm when the screen is 1.0 m from the slits.

(i) Calculate the separation between the slits.
(ii) What is the path difference at the 3rd dark fringe (in terms of lambda)?
(iii) If the screen is moved to 2.0 m, what is the new fringe width?
(iv) State how the pattern changes if white light replaces the monochromatic light.
questions.answer:
(i) beta = lambda D/d => d = lambda D/beta = (500e-9 x 1.0)/(1.0e-3) = 5 x 10^-4 m = 0.5 mm.
(ii) The m-th dark fringe has path difference (m - 1/2)*lambda; for the 3rd dark fringe (m = 3) the path difference is (3 - 1/2)*lambda = 2.5 lambda = 5*lambda/2.
(iii) beta is proportional to D, so doubling D to 2.0 m doubles the fringe width to 2.0 mm.
(iv) With white light the central fringe is white, and the fringes on either side become coloured (violet nearest the centre, red farthest), because the fringe width depends on wavelength; only a few coloured fringes are seen before they overlap.
questions.explanation: d = 0.5 mm; path diff = 2.5 lambda; beta doubles to 2.0 mm; white central + coloured fringes.

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the questions.

A parallel beam of light of wavelength 500 nm is incident normally on a single slit of width 0.5 mm. The diffraction pattern is observed on a screen 1.0 m away.

(i) State the condition for the first minimum.
(ii) Find the distance of the first minimum from the centre of the pattern.
(iii) Find the width of the central maximum.
(iv) Compare this diffraction pattern with the interference pattern of a double slit in one respect.
questions.answer:
(i) First minimum: a sin theta = lambda, i.e. a sin theta = 1 x lambda.
(ii) For small angles, y1 = D lambda/a = (1.0 x 500e-9)/(0.5e-3) = (5e-7)/(5e-4) = 1.0 x 10^-3 m = 1.0 mm from the centre.
(iii) Width of central maximum = 2 y1 = 2 D lambda/a = 2.0 mm.
(iv) In the single-slit diffraction pattern the central maximum is much wider and brighter than the side bands and the bands are unequally spaced/unequal in brightness; in a double-slit interference pattern the bright fringes are equally spaced and (ideally) equally bright.
questions.explanation: First minimum a sin theta = lambda; y1 = 1 mm; central width 2 mm; diffraction unequal vs interference equal.
